hub.description: Area guide for Northern BC: EnerGuide home energy audits, CSA F280-12 heat loss calculations, radon, mould, well water and WETT inspections across 11 communities, with local health-unit, climate and housing data.
hub.lede: The Fraser-Fort George and Peace River regional districts are home to 158,511 people (2021 Census), 123,038 of them in the eleven municipalities listed here, and 11% of their houses were built before 1961. This guide covers 11 communities, from Prince George, Dawson Creek and Fort St. John to the smallest hamlets, with the local numbers that shape an energy audit or a home health test.

cards.text: 158,511 people and 72,060 private dwellings in 2021, up 0.7% in population since 2016. On census day (May 11, 2021), 10% of the 72,060 private dwellings in the Fraser-Fort George and Peace River regional districts were not anyone's permanent home.

Of the 42,520 houses in the eleven municipalities listed here (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses, duplexes and mobile homes), 11% were built before 1961 and 69% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. The typical house dates from 1971–1980.

Environment and Climate Change Canada's 1981–2010 climate normal at Prince George STP (4.0 km from Prince George) is 4,673 heating degree-days a year, with a January mean of −6.7°C. At Dawson Creek Airport, 4.0 km from Dawson Creek, the normal is 5,870 heating degree-days, with a January mean of −13.2°C. The building code's 2.5% January design temperatures for the area run from −32°C to −38°C.

In Health Canada’s 2012 survey, 12% of 208 homes tested in the Northern Interior Health Service Delivery Area were above the guideline; 10% of 200 homes tested in the Northeast Health Service Delivery Area were above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports about 1 in 3 homes at or above the guideline for the survey's B.C. Interior region (northern and interior B.C.).
NRCan's list (checked October 8, 2026) shows 16 service organizations registered for postal codes in Prince George, Dawson Creek and Fort St. John. Confirm they travel to your community.

home-energy-audit.h1: Home energy audits in Northern BC
home-energy-audit.title: Home energy audits and EnerGuide evaluations in Northern BC: Prince George, Dawson Creek, Fort St. John
home-energy-audit.description: Book a home energy assessment (EnerGuide evaluation) in Northern BC: 16 NRCan-registered organizations list Prince George, Dawson Creek and Fort St. John postal codes, 69% of local houses predate 1991, plus B.C. rebates.
home-energy-audit.lede: 16 NRCan-registered service organizations list postal codes in Prince George, Dawson Creek and Fort St. John, and 69% of the 42,520 houses in Northern BC were built before 1991. Here's what an EnerGuide evaluation costs, what it tends to find in local houses, and which British Columbia rebates it unlocks, from Prince George, Dawson Creek and Fort St. John to the smallest hamlet.

glance.sub: for Prince George, Dawson Creek and 1 more

sections.h2: What an evaluation finds in Northern BC
sections.html:
Of the 42,520 houses in the eleven municipalities listed here (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses, duplexes and mobile homes), 11% were built before 1961 and 69% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. The typical house here dates from 1971–1980. An EnerGuide evaluation is how you find out what that means for yours: the blower door measures air leakage, the advisor inspects the attic, walls, basement, windows and heating system, and the report ranks upgrades by what they'd save.

Environment and Climate Change Canada's 1981–2010 climate normal at Prince George STP (4.0 km from Prince George) is 4,673 heating degree-days a year, with a January mean of −6.7°C. The more heating a climate needs, the more each fix is worth, which is why the ranked list in the report matters.

On census day (May 11, 2021), 10% of the 72,060 private dwellings in the Fraser-Fort George and Peace River regional districts were not anyone's permanent home. If you're evaluating a cottage or a house you're about to buy, tell the advisor how and when it's heated; the report models the house as a year-round home.

sections.h2: What it costs in Northern BC
sections.html:
There's no provincial price list; the City of Nanaimo quotes $400–$500 as typical for an existing home.

Most providers quote the initial (pre-upgrade) and follow-up (post-upgrade) visits separately, and organizations based in a city may add a travel fee for rural addresses. Rebate programs that pay on measured improvement need both visits, so ask for the combined price, travel included.

sections.h2: How a home energy assessment works
sections.html:
• Initial evaluation, about 2–3 hours. The advisor measures and inspects the house and runs the blower door test.
  • Report and EnerGuide rating. You get the home's energy rating and a list of recommended upgrades with estimated savings.
  • Do the work. Most rebate programs only count upgrades done after the initial evaluation.
  • Follow-up evaluation. A second visit measures the improvement, which is what most rebates pay on.

Read more: What a home energy audit involves.

faq.a: NRCan's list (checked October 8, 2026) shows 16 organizations registered for postal codes in Prince George, Dawson Creek and Fort St. John; 10 of them list all 3. Confirm they travel to your community before you book.

faq.q: How long does an EnerGuide evaluation take?
faq.a: The initial visit usually takes two to three hours, including the blower door test. The follow-up visit after upgrades is shorter.

faq.q: Is a home energy audit worth it for an older house in Northern BC?
faq.a: 69% of local houses were built before 1991 (2021 Census), and the area averages about 4,673 heating degree-days a year. Older houses in a cold climate are where a ranked upgrade list pays off most, and most rebates need the evaluation first.

faq.a: Currently: BC Home Energy Improvement Bonus ($20 for every percentage-point your home improves — $750 minimum, $2,000 maximum — or $300 for any two upgrades). Check the program page for current terms before you book.

heat-loss-calculation.h1: Heat loss calculations in Northern BC
heat-loss-calculation.title: CSA F280-12 heat loss calculations in Northern BC: Prince George, Dawson Creek, Fort St. John
heat-loss-calculation.description: Room-by-room CSA F280-12 heat loss calculations for Northern BC homes, sized to design temperatures of −32°C to −38°C: why it matters for heat pumps, what it costs and who does it locally.
heat-loss-calculation.lede: A heat loss calculation is how a heat pump or furnace gets sized, and its key input is the design temperature. In Northern BC, the National Building Code's 2.5% January design temperatures run from −32°C at Prince George to −38°C at Dawson Creek, so a calculation for a house near Dawson Creek starts from a colder number than one near Prince George. Here's what that means for Prince George, Dawson Creek and Fort St. John and the rest of the area.

sections.html:
The National Building Code of Canada 2020 says the 2.5% January design temperature is the value ordinarily used to design heating systems. Its climate table lists these British Columbia locations in or next to Northern BC:

Location in the code’s tableJanuary 2.5% design temperatureHeating degree-days
Prince George−32°C4,720
Mackenzie−34°C5,550
Dawson Creek−38°C5,900
Fort St. John−35°C5,750
Chetwynd−35°C5,500
Taylor−35°C5,720

Environment and Climate Change Canada's 1981–2010 climate normal at Prince George STP (4.0 km from Prince George) is 4,673 heating degree-days a year, with a January mean of −6.7°C. At Dawson Creek Airport, 4.0 km from Dawson Creek, the normal is 5,870 heating degree-days, with a January mean of −13.2°C.

The code requires the heating capacity for a house to be worked out with CSA F280, using the code's own design temperatures, and its list of referenced documents names the 2012 edition, CSA F280-12. The calculation works out how much heat each room loses on the design day, from the house's actual walls, windows, ceiling insulation and air leakage.

At −38°C, even cold-climate heat pumps lose capacity just when you need heat most. The room-by-room number tells you how much the heat pump can cover and how much backup heat to plan for, instead of guessing from square footage.

In B.C., the provincial Home Renovation Rebate's heat pump requirements call for a CSA F280 heat load calculation, so ask for the report with your quote.

sections.h2: What the calculation needs from your house
sections.html:
Of the 42,520 houses in the eleven municipalities listed here (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses, duplexes and mobile homes), 11% were built before 1961 and 69% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. In an older or renovated house, the walls, windows and air leakage rarely match the original plans, so ask the designer to measure rather than assume. Have this ready:

  • Room dimensions and ceiling heights, or a floor plan.
  • Window and door sizes and types, room by room.
  • Insulation levels in the attic, walls, basement and any floor over an unheated space.
  • A blower door result from an EnerGuide evaluation, if you've had one.
  • Where the ducts, radiators or baseboards run, so the heat can be delivered room by room.

There's no standard published price for a standalone F280 calculation, so ask two or three providers for a written quote that names the deliverable: the room-by-room F280 report, not just an equipment size. Many energy advisors bundle it with an EnerGuide evaluation, which also gives the calculation measured air-leakage data instead of an assumption. Ask whether a rural travel fee applies. The CSA F280 heat-loss calculation explains the method and typical cost bands.

faq.q: What design temperature is used for heat pump sizing in Prince George?
faq.a: The National Building Code 2020's climate table gives −32°C for Prince George, −34°C for Mackenzie, −38°C for Dawson Creek, −35°C for Fort St. John, −35°C for Chetwynd and −35°C for Taylor. Provincial codes can use their own climate tables, so ask which value the calculation uses.

faq.q: What is CSA F280-12?
faq.a: The 2012 edition of CSA F280, Determining the required capacity of residential space heating and cooling appliances. The National Building Code 2020 requires heating capacity for a house to be determined with it.

faq.q: How much does a heat loss calculation cost?
faq.a: There is no standard published price. Ask two or three providers for a written quote for the F280 report, and ask whether it costs less bundled with an EnerGuide evaluation and whether a travel fee applies.

faq.q: Who does F280 calculations in Northern BC?
faq.a: Many of the 16 NRCan-registered organizations that list Prince George, Dawson Creek and Fort St. John postal codes offer them, as do HVAC designers. Ask for the F280 report itself, not just an equipment size.

radon-testing.h1: Radon testing and long-term monitoring in Northern BC
radon-testing.kicker: British Columbia · Home health · area guide
radon-testing.title: Radon testing and long-term monitoring in Northern BC: Prince George, Dawson Creek, Fort St. John
radon-testing.description: Radon in Northern BC: 12% of 208 homes tested in the Northern Interior Health Service Delivery Area were above the guideline in Health Canada's survey. How to run a 91-day long-term test, where to borrow a monitor, and mitigation by C-NRPP professionals.
radon-testing.lede: Radon is invisible, has no smell, and is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in Canada. In Health Canada's national survey, 12% of 208 homes tested in the Northern Interior Health Service Delivery Area were above the guideline; the larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports about 1 in 3 homes at or above the guideline for the survey's B.C. Interior region (northern and interior B.C.). Only a long-term test tells you about your own house, in Prince George, Dawson Creek and Fort St. John or anywhere else in Northern BC.

glance.sub: B.C. Interior region (northern and interior B.C.)

sections.html:
In Health Canada’s 2012 survey, 12% of 208 homes tested in the Northern Interior Health Service Delivery Area were above the guideline; 10% of 200 homes tested in the Northeast Health Service Delivery Area were above the guideline.

The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports about 1 in 3 homes at or above the guideline for the survey's B.C. Interior region (northern and interior B.C.). The two surveys aren't directly comparable: the 2024 study pooled about 69,000 volunteer tests, more of them in basements, which partly explains its higher numbers. Neither can tell you about a single house, because neighbouring homes can differ widely.

sections.h2: Long-term monitoring: how to test properly
sections.html:
Health Canada's measurement guide asks for a long-term test with at least 91 days in the heating season, when closed windows and the stack effect make readings higher, so the result is a conservative estimate of the yearly average. It recommends testing for 3 to 12 months.

  • Alpha track detectors record radon's alpha particles on a plastic film; you mail them to a lab when the test ends.
  • Electret ion chambers lose charge as radon ionizes the air inside; a lab reads the voltage drop.
  • Digital (electronic) monitors read continuously and show results on a screen or an app. For a long-term test, Health Canada says to use one that has passed C-NRPP performance testing, and it still has to run at least three months.

Place the detector on the lowest level where someone spends more than four hours a day, at least 30 cm above the floor and 30 cm from walls, and at least 1 m from vents, windows and doors; avoid kitchens, laundry rooms and bathrooms. A digital monitor left running after mitigation lets you watch for changes between the long-term tests below.

• BC Lung's library lending program puts radon detectors in many BC libraries, free with a library card, and the BC Centre for Disease Control publishes a BC Radon Map of results by area.
  • For a professional measurement or mitigation, search the C-NRPP directory ↗ by postal code; it lists certified measurement and mitigation professionals, and you can confirm they cover Prince George and the rest of Northern BC.

sections.h2: If your level is high: mitigation
sections.html:
Health Canada recommends fixing levels above 200 Bq/m³ within a year, and sooner the higher the level. The usual fix is a sub-slab depressurization system (a sealed pipe through the floor and a fan venting outside), which Health Canada says costs about $2,000 to $3,000 including material and labour and cuts radon by more than 80% in most homes. Hire a professional certified for mitigation under C-NRPP.

After a system goes in:

  • A C-NRPP professional runs a short test starting at least 24 hours after the fan is turned on.
  • A long-term three-month test follows in the next fall or winter, done by a company other than the installer.
  • With an active system, Health Canada recommends a long-term test within two years of activation and every five years after that, and again after renovations.
  • Check the system's pressure gauge (manometer) regularly and never switch the fan off. It costs about $50 to $75 a year to run; a replacement fan is $200 to $300.

Since March 2024, the BC Building Code requires a radon rough-in in all new houses province-wide. The Canadian Lung Association's Lungs Matter program offers up to $1,500 toward mitigation for households with low to moderate incomes or a lung cancer diagnosis.

Read more: The radon testing guide.

faq.q: Is radon a problem in Northern BC?
faq.a: In Health Canada’s 2012 survey, 12% of 208 homes tested in the Northern Interior Health Service Delivery Area were above the guideline; 10% of 200 homes tested in the Northeast Health Service Delivery Area were above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports about 1 in 3 homes at or above the guideline for the survey's B.C. Interior region (northern and interior B.C.). Any home can have high radon, so Health Canada recommends testing every home.

faq.q: How long should a radon test take?
faq.a: At least three months, with at least 91 days in the heating season. Health Canada recommends 3 to 12 months; short tests can’t give your long-term average.

faq.q: Where can I get a radon monitor or kit in Prince George?
faq.a: BC Lung's library lending program puts radon detectors in many BC libraries, free with a library card, and the BC Centre for Disease Control publishes a BC Radon Map of results by area. Long-term kits are also sold online and at hardware stores.

faq.q: What does radon mitigation cost?
faq.a: Health Canada puts a sub-slab depressurization system at about $2,000 to $3,000 including material and labour, plus about $50 to $75 a year to run the fan.

faq.q: Should I keep monitoring after mitigation?
faq.a: Yes. Health Canada recommends a long-term test the following heating season, another within two years of activation, and one every five years after that. A digital monitor running in between shows if anything changes.

mold-testing.h1: Mould and indoor air quality testing in Northern BC
mold-testing.kicker: British Columbia · Home health · area guide
mold-testing.title: Mould and indoor air quality (IAQ) testing in Northern BC: Prince George, Dawson Creek, Fort St. John
mold-testing.description: Mould inspection and indoor air quality testing in Northern BC, where 69% of houses were built before 1991: when mold sampling helps, the cleanup size rules from CMHC and Health Canada, and when to hire a remediation contractor.
mold-testing.lede: 69% of the 42,520 houses in Northern BC were built before 1991, and winters here bring about 4,673 heating degree-days a year: cold corners and older basements are where mould usually starts. Here's how to inspect for it in Prince George, Dawson Creek and Fort St. John, when air sampling helps, and when cleanup is a job for a contractor.

glance.sub: or if it keeps coming back

sections.h2: Why mould shows up in Northern BC homes
sections.html:
Environment and Climate Change Canada's 1981–2010 climate normal at Prince George STP (4.0 km from Prince George) is 4,673 heating degree-days a year, with a January mean of −6.7°C. On cold days, exterior corners, closets on outside walls and window frames get cold enough for condensation, which is where mould often starts.

Of the 42,520 houses in the eleven municipalities listed here (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses, duplexes and mobile homes), 11% were built before 1961 and 69% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older basements without a moisture barrier, and houses air-sealed without adding ventilation, are common trouble spots.

On census day (May 11, 2021), 10% of the 72,060 private dwellings in the Fraser-Fort George and Peace River regional districts were not anyone's permanent home. A house or cottage that sits closed up for long stretches is worth a sniff test and a look in the basement each time you open it.

Start by looking and smelling: stains, discoloured patches, peeling paint and a musty odour, especially in basements, bathrooms, window frames and closets on outside walls. Health Canada says measuring mould concentrations or identifying species is usually unnecessary: if you can see or smell it, fix the moisture and clean up.

Air or surface sampling helps when you smell mustiness but can't find the source, after a leak or flood to check the cleanup worked, or before buying a house with signs of past water damage. Ask which lab analyzes the samples and look for one accredited under AIHA's EMLAP program.

sections.h2: Cleanup and remediation: the size rules
sections.html:
CMHC and Health Canada sort mould by size, and the size decides who should clean it up:

SizeWhat countsWho should clean it
SmallOne to three patches, each smaller than 1 m²A healthy homeowner, with water and unscented dish detergent (CMHC)
MediumMore than three patches, or patches between 1 and 3 m² (32 square feet)Trained help; homeowners only with training and precautions
LargeA patch larger than 3 m², or many patches through the houseA qualified mould remediation contractor (CMHC)
  • Fix the moisture source first: a leak, poor drainage, or condensation from high humidity. Health Canada recommends 30–50% relative humidity.
  • For a small cleanup, wear safety glasses or goggles, an N95 mask if possible and household rubber gloves. People at risk from mould shouldn't clean it and should stay away.
  • Health Canada suggests professional help for extensive mould, especially growth that keeps coming back after cleaning.

Ask any tester which lab analyzes their samples and what the report will recommend; a good report points to the moisture source. For remediation, get two or three written quotes that describe containment, what will be removed and how the area is cleaned. No province has a mandatory mould standard for homes, and Health Canada sets no numerical limit.

Read more: The mould and indoor air quality guide.

faq.q: Do I need mould testing in Northern BC if I can see mould?
faq.a: Usually not. Visible mould needs cleanup and a fix for the moisture source. Sampling helps most when you suspect mould you can’t see.

faq.q: How much mould can I clean myself?
faq.a: CMHC says a healthy homeowner can clean one to three patches, each under 1 m², with water and unscented dish detergent. Larger areas need trained help or a remediation contractor.

faq.q: When should I hire a mould remediation contractor?
faq.a: For a single patch over 3 m², many patches through the house, or mould that keeps coming back after cleaning (CMHC, Health Canada).

faq.q: Is there a legal mould limit for homes in Canada?
faq.a: No. Health Canada sets no numerical limit; its guidance is to control moisture and clean up mould.

well-water-testing.h1: Well water testing in Northern BC
well-water-testing.kicker: British Columbia · Home health · area guide
well-water-testing.title: Well water testing in Northern BC: E. coli and coliform tests in Prince George, Dawson Creek, Fort St. John
well-water-testing.description: Private well water testing in Northern BC: bacteria (E. coli and total coliforms) and chemistry through a qualified lab, how often B.C. recommends testing, what Northern Health says, and what to do if a test comes back positive.
well-water-testing.lede: There's no free provincial well-testing program in B.C., so well owners in Northern BC, from Prince George, Dawson Creek and Fort St. John to rural acreages, use a qualified lab. Northern Health tests permitted water systems, not individual homes. Here's what to test for, how often, how to choose a lab, and what to do if bacteria show up.

sections.h2: Testing a well in Northern BC
sections.html: There's no free provincial program: use a qualified lab (search the CALA directory), which supplies the bottles. HealthLinkBC recommends testing for bacteria at least once a year and for chemistry when the well is new and annually after that.

• Bacteria (total coliforms and E. coli): at least once a year, and right away if the water's clarity, colour or taste changes.
  • Chemistry when the well is new and every year after: HealthLinkBC names nitrates, fluoride and metals such as arsenic, lead, copper and manganese as the most common concerns in B.C. groundwater.

Search the CALA directory for an accredited lab near you; the lab supplies sterile bottles and instructions, and charges for the analysis. Read the instructions carefully and follow them exactly, and keep every result for future reference.

sections.h2: What Northern Health does, and doesn’t do
sections.html: Northern Health looks after water testing for permitted water systems but doesn't test individual homes, and it doesn't recommend specific labs: any accredited lab in B.C. will do. It says private supplies should be tested for bacteria at least once a year, that chemical results show whether anything exceeds health standards or aesthetic objectives, and that a local environmental health officer can help you interpret results or find a certified lab. It also notes that contaminants can get into a well through cracks in the casing, poorly fitted lids or other structural faults, and that a well close to sources of pollution can pick up bacteria, nitrates or other chemicals.

HealthLinkBC says water with E. coli is not safe to drink: treat it before drinking, preparing food or brushing teeth (boiling is a short-term option), then find and fix the source, with long-term treatment if the source can't be corrected. Total coliforms without E. coli can mean the well needs better sanitation or physical upgrades, or that surface water may be getting in. Re-test after floods, drought or similar events, and don't rely on a neighbour's result: a safe test next door doesn't mean your water is safe.

Before disinfecting, the province's guide to simple chlorination asks you to check the wellhead:

  • Sewage sources near the well, such as manure or compost piles or a septic field.
  • Ground that slopes toward the well or lets water pond around it.
  • A missing, cracked or damaged well cap, or one that lets water or vermin in.
  • Casing that sticks up less than 30 cm (1 ft) above the ground or pump-house floor, or a gap or cracks in the seal around it.

Fix those first, or the well stays vulnerable. A registered well driller or pump installer has to do any surface-seal repair or casing extension, and the guide warns that chlorine vapour is dangerous in confined spaces such as pump houses, well pits and crawl spaces.

Read more: The well water guide.

faq.q: Is well water testing free in Northern BC?
faq.a: No. B.C. has no free provincial program; a qualified lab charges for the analysis and supplies the bottles.

faq.q: How often should I test my well?
faq.a: HealthLinkBC recommends bacteria testing at least once a year, and chemistry when the well is new and every year after.

faq.q: What chemicals should I test for?
faq.a: HealthLinkBC names nitrates, fluoride and metals such as arsenic, lead, copper and manganese as the most common chemicals of concern in B.C. groundwater.

faq.q: Where do I find a lab?
faq.a: Search the CALA directory of accredited laboratories; the lab provides the bottles and instructions.

faq.q: What if my well water test shows E. coli?
faq.a: HealthLinkBC says the water is not safe to drink. Treat it before drinking, cooking or brushing teeth (boiling works short term), find and fix the source, and disinfect the well once the wellhead is sound.

wood-burning-inspection.h1: Wood-burning appliance inspections (WETT) in Northern BC
wood-burning-inspection.kicker: British Columbia · Home health · area guide
wood-burning-inspection.title: WETT-certified wood stove and chimney inspections in Northern BC: Prince George, Dawson Creek, Fort St. John
wood-burning-inspection.description: Wood-burning appliance (WETT) inspections in Northern BC: what an inspection checks, how to find a WETT-certified inspector, certified stoves, and the National Fire Code rule for a chimney inspection every 12 months.
wood-burning-inspection.lede: The National Fire Code requires every chimney, flue and flue pipe to be inspected at least once every 12 months, when an appliance is added and after any chimney fire. In Northern BC, with about 4,673 heating degree-days a year, a wood stove or insert can run for much of the year. Here's what an inspection covers and how to book a WETT-certified inspector in Prince George, Dawson Creek and Fort St. John or anywhere else in the area.

sections.h2: Why inspections matter in Northern BC
sections.html:
Environment and Climate Change Canada's 1981–2010 climate normal at Prince George STP (4.0 km from Prince George) is 4,673 heating degree-days a year, with a January mean of −6.7°C. Of the 42,520 houses in the eleven municipalities listed here (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses, duplexes and mobile homes), 11% were built before 1961 and 69% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

On census day (May 11, 2021), 10% of the 72,060 private dwellings in the Fraser-Fort George and Peace River regional districts were not anyone's permanent home. If you're buying a cottage or a house with a wood stove, ask your insurer what inspection it needs before the deal closes.

WETT Inc., the non-profit that trains and registers wood-energy professionals across Canada, says hiring a WETT-certified professional ensures wood-burning appliances are inspected, installed and maintained to current safety codes and standards, and helps homeowners meet insurance or regulatory requirements.

An inspection looks at what the fire and installation codes regulate:

  • The chimney, flue and flue pipe: structural problems such as a missing liner or inadequate supports, and decay such as cracking, crumbling mortar, corrosion or separated sections (National Fire Code notes).
  • Creosote and soot: deposits more than 3 mm thick mean the chimney needs cleaning right away and should be inspected more often.
  • Clearances: the required space between the appliance, flue pipe or chimney and anything combustible, which must be kept clear.
  • The installation: CSA B365 is the installation code for solid-fuel appliances, covering installation, alteration and maintenance.
  • The appliance itself: whether it's certified to CSA B415.1 or the US EPA standard, which you can usually tell from its label or plate.

Search the WETT directory ↗ for certified professionals near Prince George and the rest of Northern BC, and ask your home insurer what it needs to see when you add a stove or buy a house that has one. WETT doesn't publish inspection prices, so get two or three written quotes and ask what each inspection includes.

B.C.'s Solid Fuel Burning Domestic Appliance Regulation sets standards for wood stoves and other wood-burning appliances sold in the province, and the Community Wood Smoke Reduction Program offers incentives to replace old wood stoves with cleaner heating (gas and propane exchanges ended January 1, 2023). The province's list of local programs includes the Prince George Community Wood Smoke Reduction Program (Prince George and unincorporated areas of the Regional District of Fraser-Fort George) and programs in Mackenzie and Valemount. We found no listing for the Peace River Regional District.

• Burn dry wood: the US EPA says wood burns best below 20% moisture; check it with a moisture meter.
  • Dense smoke at the top of the chimney is a warning sign of poor operation, a wrongly sized chimney or unsuitable fuel (National Fire Code note).
  • Keep combustible things out of the clearance space around the stove and flue pipe.
  • Have the chimney inspected after any chimney fire, and when you add or replace an appliance.

Read the full wood-burning inspection guide.

faq.q: How often should a wood stove chimney be inspected in Northern BC?
faq.a: The National Fire Code requires every chimney, flue and flue pipe to be inspected at least once every 12 months, when an appliance is added and after any chimney fire, and cleaned as often as needed to keep combustible deposits from building up.

faq.q: What is a WETT inspection?
faq.a: An inspection of a wood-burning appliance and its chimney or venting by a professional certified through the WETT program, which WETT Inc. says helps homeowners meet insurance or regulatory requirements.

faq.q: How do I find a WETT-certified inspector near Prince George?
faq.a: Search the WETT directory on wettinc.ca, then confirm the inspector covers your address and ask what the inspection includes.

faq.q: How much does a WETT inspection cost?
faq.a: WETT doesn’t publish prices and we found no reliable published range, so ask two or three inspectors for written quotes.

faq.q: What is a certified wood stove?
faq.a: One tested to CSA B415.1 or certified by the US EPA for emissions. The EPA’s 2020 limit for new room heaters is 2.0 grams of particles per hour (crib wood) or 2.5 g/h (cord wood).
